nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the silver-fork novel and the fashionable stage
literary_identity: Novelist and playwright; the most expert writer of the silver-fork novel of fashionable life and the author of more than seventy novels.
biography: Born Catherine Grace Frances Moody in London in 1799; she married an army officer in 1823 and, after his death, supported her family by her pen. Her novels of fashionable life — Cecil (1841), The Money-Lender (1843), Skittles (1845) — and her plays made her the most expert chronicler of the aristocracy of the 1830s and 1840s. She died in London on 29 January 1861.
literary_profile: Catherine Gore was the most expert writer of the silver-fork novel of fashionable life and one of the most prolific novelists of the early Victorian period: her seventy-odd books recorded the aristocracy at play with a precision that makes her the central social novelist of the 1830s and 1840s.
stylistic_characteristics: The fashionable assembly and the great house; the epigram and the smart dialogue; the satirical portrait of the aristocracy; the stage comedy of manners; the rapid, witty, well-bred prose.
intellectual_concerns: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income; money, credit, speculation, and the joint-stock imagination; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Irish-British; the conversational memoir and the fashionable salon
literary_identity: Novelist, memoirist and salon hostess; the author of Conversations with Lord Byron and one of the most celebrated women of letters of the 1830s.
biography: Born Margaret Power near Clonmel in 1789; she married Captain Maurice Farmer at fifteen, left him, and married the Earl of Blessington in 1818; the couple travelled in Europe, where she met Lord Byron in Genoa. Conversations with Lord Byron (1834), The Idler in Italy (1839) and her novels followed, and she presided over the most famous salon in London. She died in Paris on 4 June 1849.
literary_profile: The Countess of Blessington was one of the most celebrated women of letters of the 1830s and her salon the centre of literary London: Conversations with Lord Byron is a central document of the poet's last years, and The Idler in Italy created the fashionable travel book of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The reported conversation of the great man; the travel book of the fashionable tour; the comic novel of high life; the anecdote and the portrait; the confiding, graceful, society prose.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Evangelical novel and the historical romance
literary_identity: Novelist; one of the most popular Evangelical novelists of the 1830s and 1840s and a writer of spirited historical romances.
biography: Born Anne Caldwell in London in 1791; she married Lieutenant-Colonel James Marsh and wrote some thirty novels, beginning with The Admiral's Daughter (1833) and Two Old Men's Tales (1834), and including Emilia Wyndham (1846) and The Protestant Reformation in France (1847). She died in London on 2 March 1874.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the Anglo-Indian satire and the society novel
literary_identity: Novelist and traveller; the author of The Semi-Attached Couple and The Semi-Detached House, two of the wittiest society novels of the century.
biography: Born Emily Eden in Westminster on 3 March 1797, the daughter of the first Baron Auckland; she went to India with her brother Lord Auckland, the Governor-General, and her letters from the East became Up the Country (1866). The Semi-Attached Couple (1860) and The Semi-Detached House (1859) followed. She died at Richmond on 5 August 1869.
literary_profile: Emily Eden wrote two of the wittiest society novels of the nineteenth century: The Semi-Attached Couple and The Semi-Detached House are the finest English comedies of manners between Austen and Thackeray, and her Anglo-Indian letters are a central document of the British in India.
stylistic_characteristics: The comedy of the country house and the suburban villa; the epigram and the drawing-room dialogue; the satirical portrait of the aristocracy; the Anglo-Indian landscape and the voyage; the light, dry, well-bred prose.
intellectual_concerns: Leisure class, the idle rich, and the unearned income; empire, jingoism, and the literature of the metropole; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the New Woman short story
literary_identity: Short-story writer and playwright; the pseudonym of Mary Chavelita Dunne Bright, the most radical of the New Woman writers.
biography: Born Mary Chavelita Dunne in Melbourne on 14 December 1859 of Irish parents; she lived in Ireland, America and Norway, married Egerton Tertius Clairmonte in 1891, and published Keynotes in 1893. Discords (1894), Symphonies (1897) and her plays followed. She died at Haslemere on 12 August 1945.
literary_profile: George Egerton was the most radical of the New Woman writers and Keynotes the most scandalous book of the 1890s: her stories of women's sexual and emotional experience, told in a new and impressionistic prose, made her the founder of the feminist short story in English.
stylistic_characteristics: The short impressionistic story without plot; the interior monologue of the woman's desire; the refusal of the marriage ending; the Scandinavian influence of the new drama; the lyric, sensuous, disjointed prose.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; sexuality, the double standard, and the literature of the social evil; self-destruction, melancholy, and the coroner's verdict; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital.
historical_significance: George Egerton was the most radical of the New Woman writers and Keynotes the most scandalous book of the 1890s: her stories of women's sexual and emotional experience made her the founder of the feminist short story in English.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the New Woman school story and the suffrage novel
literary_identity: Novelist and children's writer; the author of The Story of a Modern Woman and one of the most important of the New Woman novelists.
biography: Born Janet Syrett at Ramsgate on 17 March 1865; she taught at the Polytechnic School for Girls, wrote for the Yellow Book, and published Nobody's Fault (1888), The Story of a Modern Woman (1894) and The Victorians (1895). She supported the suffrage movement and died at Richmond on 15 September 1943.
literary_profile: Netta Syrett wrote The Story of a Modern Woman, one of the most important New Woman novels of the 1890s: her portrait of a woman artist's struggle for independence gave the movement its finest novel of the professional woman, and her school stories made her a central figure of the girls' fiction of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The novel of the woman artist's education; the school story and the studio; the refusal of the marriage plot; the plain, ironic, realistic prose; the direct argument on the woman question.
intellectual_concerns: The woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; art versus life, and the romance of the artist; education, the schools, and the cultivation of the self; the metropolis, the crowd, and the imperial capital.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American-British; the suffrage drama and the Ibsen actress
literary_identity: Actress, novelist and suffragist; the greatest English-language actress of Ibsen and the author of Votes for Women and The New Woman.
biography: Born Elizabeth Robins in Louisville, Kentucky, on 6 August 1862; she came to London in 1885 and made her name in the first English productions of Ibsen. The New Woman (1894), Alan's Wife (1893) and Votes for Women (1907) followed, and she was a central organiser of the suffrage campaign. She died at Brighton on 8 May 1952.

biography: Born Gertrude Dix in England in 1860; she was active in the socialist and feminist circles of the 1890s and published The Image Breakers in 1900, a novel of the socialist future and the woman's place in it. Little else is recorded of her life, and she died in 1950.
